assistant_text:
Impulse and momentum are tightly linked ideas in mechanics, with impulse acting as the cause and momentum as the effect (the quantity that changes).

- How they’re related
  - Momentum: p = m v. It measures how much motion an object has.
  - Impulse: J = ∆p = ∫ F dt. It is the total effect of a force acting over a time interval.
  - If mass is constant, the impulse- momentum relation can be written as F dt = m dv, and integrating gives ∫ F dt = m (v2 − v1) = ∆p.
  - The instantaneous form is F = dp/dt, so the rate at which momentum changes is the net force.

- The multiplicative-combination substrate (how both quantities arise from a product of two factors)
  - Momentum is the product of two things: mass and velocity (p = m v). This is a classic multiplicative substrate: motion is built from “how much stuff” (mass) times “how fast” it’s moving (velocity).
  - Impulse is also built from a product, but this time of force and time (J = F Δt). The strength of the interaction (force) multiplied by how long it acts gives the total change in momentum.
  - When mass changes (e.g., a rocket losing mass), p = m v still applies, but dp/dt = F becomes dp/dt = m dv/dt + v dm/dt. The impulse integral ∆p still represents the cumulative effect of the interaction, now capturing both velocity change and any mass flow through the product structure.

- The interaction-change substrate (how interactions drive changes in momentum)
  - Force is the agent of interaction between bodies (gravity, contact, thrust, etc.). This is the mechanism that changes momentum.
  - Impulse quantifies the cumulative interaction: J = ∫ F dt. It is the total momentum transfer due to the interaction over the time interval.
  - Momentum changes only when there is a net external interaction (external impulse). In an isolated system with no external forces, the total momentum is conserved, which is another way these substrates express the same idea: interactions redistribute momentum without changing the total in the system.
  - In collisions, the impulse delivered during the interaction region equals the change in the objects’ momenta, tying the interaction-change substrate directly to momentum change.

- Quick illustrations
  - A bat hitting a ball: the force acts over a short time, producing impulse J. The ball’s momentum changes by ∆p = J (and p = m v for the ball afterward).
  - A rocket: exhaust mass leaves the rocket, mass changes while thrust acts. The rocket’s momentum changes according to dp/dt = F, and the total impulse from the thrust over time equals the change in the rocket’s momentum, even though both mass and velocity are changing.

In short, impulse and momentum are two faces of the same coin: momentum changes because of interactions, and impulse measures the accumulated effect of those interactions. Both concepts rely on the same underlying substrates—multiplicative combinations (mass×velocity for momentum; force×time for impulse) and interaction-driven changes (forces causing changes in momentum).

task_contract.semantic_unit: Describe how impulse and momentum are related, and explain how both reuse the multiplicative-combination and interaction-change substrates.
